summary:
Tempo is a readiness tool for lunar surface crews. It links astronaut health monitoring directly to the spacewalk schedule. Artemis missions will pack several demanding EVAs into a few days, and on long missions astronauts carry much of the responsibility for spotting changes in their own health. Tempo makes those changes visible and actionable.

In two minutes, an astronaut completes a reaction-time test and a precision motor task. Tempo combines these with wearable sleep, readiness and heart-rate data and compares everything with the astronaut’s own baseline. Robust, explainable statistics flag only meaningful declines, and each flag says exactly why it was raised. A flight surgeon reviews the whole crew in Mission control. Then an optimizer built on Google OR-Tools rebuilds the multi-day EVA plan, reducing workload or adding rest while respecting qualifications and task priorities, and it explains when a request is impossible.

The result is a closed loop: measure, flag, review, re-plan. It works offline, keeps humans in charge, and uses NASA’s public EVA data for historical context.
details:
Tempo helps a lunar crew decide whether an astronaut is ready for the next spacewalk, and re-plans the mission when they aren’t. On the ISS, NASA already tests astronauts’ cognition against their own baseline. Artemis surface missions will add something new: several demanding EVAs in a few days, with little recovery time between them. Nobody connects those readiness checks to the EVA schedule. Tempo does.

How it works

  1. Measure: In two minutes, an astronaut takes a reaction-time test (modelled on the psychomotor vigilance test NASA uses on the ISS) and a precision motor task. Sleep score, readiness and heart-rate data come from a wearable rather than self-reports. Only workload is self-rated, using the six NASA-TLX dimensions.
  2. Compare: Each result is compared with that astronaut’s own baseline, not a population average. Tempo uses robust statistics: the median, the median absolute deviation and Theil–Sen trends. A change is flagged only when it is both statistically unusual and large enough to matter, and every flag has a “Why was this flagged?” explanation.
  3. Review: In Mission control, a flight surgeon sees the whole crew with flagged members first, reads the evidence and leaves notes. The doctor decides; the software only advises.
  4. Re-plan: The EVA planner uses Google OR-Tools to rebuild the multi-day EVA schedule in about a second. It can cap one astronaut’s EVA hours, lengthen rest periods or reassign tasks, and it respects qualifications, task dependencies and priorities. Every change is explained. When a request is impossible, Tempo names the exact conflicting constraints, for example removing the only comms-qualified astronaut on the day of an antenna install.
  5. Context: NASA’s public EVA dataset (US and Russian EVAs) gives historical context on EVA durations.

Benefits and intended impact
On long missions, astronauts are largely responsible for spotting changes in their own health. Tempo turns subtle declines into clear, explainable signals before they become an operational risk, and links them directly to a decision: lighten, move or keep the next EVA. It is designed for a communication delay, so the crew can act on their own and Earth can review afterwards. The same approach could support other high-tempo, safety-critical work on Earth, such as shift work, aviation and polar stations.

How it is creative
Most health tools stop at a score. Tempo closes the loop from measuring to flagging, review and re-planning on one screen. It is fully explainable by design: there is no black-box AI deciding about a person’s health, only transparent statistics and an optimizer that explains its reasoning. It also works offline, as it would need to on the Moon.

Factors we considered

  • Scientific honesty: Tempo is a prototype, not a medical device. The crew data is synthetic and generated from fixed seeds so it can be reproduced, and our tests are inspired by NASA instruments but are not validated versions of them.
  • Privacy: real wearable data stays on the local device and is never uploaded.
  • Avoiding false alarms: there are minimum change thresholds, and a baseline is used only once it has enough sessions.
  • The human in the loop: decisions stay with the crew and the doctors.
  • Usability under time pressure: each screen gives one clear status and one action.

Tools and technologies

  • Frontend: React, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS, Recharts and Lucide.
  • Backend: Python, FastAPI, SQLite, NumPy, SciPy and Google OR-Tools (CP-SAT).
  • Tests: Pytest and Vitest (90 automated tests).
  • Data: NASA’s EVA dataset and a Fitbit / Google Health export.
  • AI assistance: Claude by Anthropic, used for coding, research, data design and writing. Details are in AI_USAGE.md in the repository.
